en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of Abhayamati, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Honorary Court Attendant,
Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Recipient of the Purple Robe.
Translated by the Śramaṇa臣 (Chen) Shi-hu and others, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great saṃgha of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; like great dragon kings, they had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, were liberated through right knowledge, possessed tranquil minds, and had all reached the further shore—with the sole exception of one person, namely Ānanda.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of five hundred great bodhisattvas—each having attained all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and samādhis, and all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood.

At that time, there was a householder in Śrāvastī named Abhayadatta, who was immensely wealthy and powerful. He possessed great riches and treasures, with stores of all manner of enjoyments filling his treasuries. He was fully endowed with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, coral, conch shells, and other precious gems; he had many carriages, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, as well as numerous kinsmen, slaves, servants, attendants, and friends.
At one time, Abhayadatta was gathered together with five hundred elders, who spoke secretly among themselves: "O worthy ones!

To encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world is a rare occurrence; a human body is difficult to obtain, and the meeting of the right time is difficult to achieve. Within the Buddha's teaching, pure faith is exceedingly difficult to find."
To renounce the home life and go forth as a bhikṣu is difficult; to practice the path is even more difficult.

For those sentient beings to recognize kindness and remember to repay it is exceedingly rare; yet even if they can perform only a small portion of such deeds, they do not let them go to waste, let alone when they are extensive and manifold.

Furthermore, it is an exceedingly difficult matter for sentient beings to give rise to pure faith within the teachings of the Tathāgata, and having given rise to such faith, to further practice in accordance with those teachings.
Furthermore, it is an exceedingly difficult matter for sentient beings to be able to adorn the teachings of the Tathāgata and, moreover, to achieve liberation from saṃsāra.
Therefore, we should not seek nirvāṇa within the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; rather, we should seek nirvāṇa within the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
Thereupon, after the assembly had deliberated upon these matters with one another, they all gave rise to a vast and superior resolve, saying:
"We now all seek nirvana within the unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma; we take no pleasure in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
Then Abhayadatta, surrounded by five hundred elders, departed from the city of Śrāvastī together with them and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this matter, intentionally addressed the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, saying:
"Elders, for what reason have you come to the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"

Then the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, all rose from their seats, bared one shoulder, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Previously, when we gathered together in one place, we spoke to one another in secret:

'To encounter a Buddha appearing in the world is a rare occurrence; a human body is difficult to obtain; the convergence of the right time is difficult; and pure faith within the Buddha's teaching is extremely difficult.'"
To renounce the household life and go forth into homelessness, assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu, is already difficult; to practice the path is even more difficult.

For those sentient beings to recognize kindness and remember to repay it is exceedingly rare; yet they are able to perform even a small portion of such service without failing or losing it, let alone on a vast scale.

Furthermore, it is an exceedingly difficult matter for sentient beings to give rise to pure faith within the teaching of the Tathāgata, and having given rise to such faith, to further practice in accordance with that teaching.
Furthermore, it is an extremely difficult matter for sentient beings to be able to adorn the teachings of the Tathāgata and, moreover, to attain liberation from saṃsāra.
At this time, we should not seek nirvāṇa within the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; rather, we should seek nirvāṇa within the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
"World-Honored One!

Having deliberated upon these matters with one another, we have all resolved to give rise to a vast and supreme mind; we shall all seek nirvāṇa within the unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma, taking no pleasure in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
"By virtue of this very cause, we have come to the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
World-Honored One!
How should those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi abide?"
"Furthermore, how does one train? How does one practice?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! You elders, it is most excellent, most excellent!”
It is well that you have now come to the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of abiding in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Listen attentively and apply your minds well; I shall now speak for you.
Then, the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"O elders! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, they should train and practice in this manner, just as they abide."

"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, they should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, universally approach them, extensively embrace them, and observe their activities."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not harbor attachment to their own body or life; nor should they be attached to any dwellings, wives, children, kinsmen, food and drink, clothing, vehicles, seats, precious jewels, wealth and grain, incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, or indeed any articles of enjoyment or pleasure.

Why is this? Because many sentient beings, out of attachment to their bodies and lives, extensively create sinful karma; when the various karmas they have committed reach maturity, they fall into the evil realms and are born within the hells.
If one gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and does not cling to one's own body or life, one will be reborn in all the happy realms.
O Householders!

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and cultivate no attachment to their own body or life. Having become free from attachment to all dwellings, wives, children, kinsmen, food and drink, clothing, vehicles, seats, precious jewels, wealth and grain, incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and even all articles of enjoyment and pleasure, they should subsequently renounce everything, extensively practicing giving without seeking any karmic reward. They should abide securely in the practice of ethical discipline, pure in its three aspects, cultivate all forms of patience to full perfection, and be able to endure and subdue all harmful actions committed by sentient beings against them.
Donning the firm armor of great diligence, they are able to relinquish both body and life; abiding in tranquility with one-pointedness of mind, they remain far removed from distraction.

In this section on the discernment of all wholesome dharmas by means of supreme wisdom, one does not give rise to views such as a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a soul, an individual, or a mind-born being. One extensively performs all manner of superior practices for the sake of all; one intentionally practices giving for the sake of all sentient beings, intentionally maintains ethical discipline for the sake of all sentient beings, intentionally practices patience for the sake of all sentient beings, intentionally arouses firm diligence for the sake of all sentient beings, intentionally abides in the gates of various superior concentrations for the sake of all sentient beings, intentionally cultivates wisdom for the sake of all sentient beings, and trains in all skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since the past, we have all conceived attachment to our own bodies and lives; we have conceived attachment to all our dwellings, wives, children, kinsmen, food and drink, clothing, vehicles, couches and seats, precious jewels, wealth and grain, incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, even unto all articles of enjoyment and pleasure.
"Bhagavān! What kind of contemplation does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perform so that they do not give rise to attachment toward their body, life, or even all objects of enjoyment and pleasure?"
“I pray that the Buddha will explain this for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, saying:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe the body through countless kinds of characteristics.”
What are these countless [reflections]?
They are as follows:
this body is unreal, a collection of conditioned dharmas like a mass of atoms; from the crown of the head to the feet, it is to be dismantled step by step.
From those nine orifices and all the pores, impurities flow forth like a swarm of ants;
within them dwell serpent poisons that cause harm and affliction;
they are like enemies and like monkeys, causing much damage and distress.
Like an extremely evil friend, they constantly give rise to contention;
the body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped or rubbed;
and it is also like a water bubble, existing for a moment and then immediately breaking.
Furthermore, it is like a mirage, produced by the thirst of craving;
like a plantain tree, which has no solid core within;
and like a magical illusion, arising from falsehood.
Furthermore, it is like a king who issues many various edicts;
it is like an adversary who constantly comes to watch for an opportunity;
and it is like a thief who possesses no sense of honor or trustworthiness.
Furthermore, it is like a murderer, exceedingly difficult to subdue;
like a wicked friend, who is never pleased;
like one who destroys the Dharma, who causes the life-force of wisdom to vanish.
Furthermore, it is like an evil companion who causes the decline and loss of wholesome dharmas;
it is like an empty village, devoid of a sovereign master;
and it is like a clay vessel, which ultimately ends in destruction.
It is like a cesspool filled with impurities;
it is like a latrine, constantly abounding in filth;
and it is like various ghosts that devour impure things, as well as maggots, dogs, and the like, who delight in stench and filth.
Furthermore, it is like a vast accumulation of filth from which the stench is smelled from afar;
like a malignant ulcer whose opening is difficult to close and whose pain is unbearable;
and like a poisoned arrow that has entered the body, causing piercing agony.
They are like a wicked master, difficult to serve and support;
or like a dilapidated house or a leaking ship, which, despite being temporarily repaired, soon returns to ruin;
or like an unbaked earthen vessel, difficult to preserve and cherish.
Furthermore, it is like an evil friend who constantly feigns protection;
like a tree on a riverbank shaken by the wind;
like a great river that ultimately flows into the sea of death.
Furthermore, it is like a guest house, where many kinds of disturbances and vexations arise;
it is like a masterless house, with nothing to provide protection or belonging;
it is like a patrolman, who is constantly and exclusively engaged in inspection.
Furthermore, it is like a frontier region where there is much harassment;
like a place where sand has been piled up that will gradually diminish and sink;
or like a spreading fire.
Like the ocean, it is difficult to cross;
like the earth, it is difficult to level;
like a snake placed in a basket, it brings harm as soon as it is born.
Furthermore, it is like an infant who must always be cherished;
like a broken vessel, which is incapable of any use;
and like a wicked place, where one must constantly fear ruin and disorder.
It is like food mixed with poison, which one should always avoid;
it is like a beggar who obtains various things and discards them immediately upon receiving them;
and it is also like a great cart carrying an extremely heavy burden.
O wise ones! Regarding the realization of the Dharma, you should understand it in this way.

The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of Abhayamati, translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven,

and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, who was conferred the purple robe. Volume Two.
The Śramaṇa臣 (臣) Fa-hu and others, by imperial decree, translated: "Furthermore, householder!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates this body: by what primary cause was it originally established?"
This means that its cause arises from the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood;

furthermore, it is sustained by the intake of food and drink, which, once consumed and transformed, immediately aggregate and then disperse, returning to the placental covering (*kalala*). As this placental covering flows with moisture, it ultimately results in impurity.
Thereafter, the element of fire increases in intensity, cooking and transforming [the elements] until they reach maturity.

Subsequently, they are returned to the power of wind; by that wind-power, the heavy dregs and the flowing moisture are each separated—the heavy dregs being what are known as feces and urine, and the flowing moisture being blood. Blood transforms into flesh; flesh becomes fat; fat becomes bone; bone produces marrow; and marrow produces semen. From semen and the other constituents, this impure body is then formed.
Because the Bodhisattva contemplates this body as impure, he gives rise to this reflection:

"This body is a composite of many diverse parts, each with its own distinct name and characteristic: namely, three hundred bones; sixty layers of adipose tissue and fat; four hundred membranes; five hundred masses of flesh; six hundred brains; seven hundred vessels; nine hundred sinews; and sixteen ribs."

Furthermore, there are three things that entwine the intestines internally: the raw, the cooked, and the visceral organs. There are sixteen cross-linked networks through which they reside; two thousand five hundred channels of the pulse permeate and reflect upon one hundred and seven joints.
Eighty million *koṭis* of pores possess the five sense organs, nine apertures, and seven internal repositories (*kośa*), all filled with impurities.

There is one handful of marrow, one handful of brain, three handfuls of fat, six handfuls of lymph, and six handfuls of heavy dregs; the force of the wind pervades everywhere, and there is one peck of blood—all such things are each fully present.

There are seven water-vessels that surround it once more; they suck up all essential nutrients, causing the internal fire to increase greatly, burning and boiling with intense heat. Under this oppressive exhaustion, the bodily vessels flow with sweat—these various signs are extremely difficult to perceive.
Regarding this foul, impure physical form, how could one give rise to superior attachment toward it?
It is like a beggar who obtains an object for use and discards it immediately upon receiving it;
or like a great cart carrying an extremely heavy load.
"O wise ones! Regarding the realization of the Dharma, you should know it thus.
He then spoke in verse:
"This body is a manifold collection of impurities, yet the ignorant and witless do not perceive it;
they forcibly give rise to a heart of intense attachment, like a foul jar that, when broken, releases a multitude of stinking odors."
The ears, eyes, mouth, and nose are all filthy; among them, what could possibly be fragrant and pure?
With saliva, eye-secretions, wax, and mucus—amidst such a mixture of worms and impurities, how can one give rise to attachment?
For example, it is like a fool who takes up charcoal and exerts great effort to polish it, desiring to make it white;
though the charcoal is exhausted and his strength is spent, no whiteness is achieved. So too is the case with the deluded greed of those lacking wisdom.
Just as when a person desires to achieve purity, they perform many kinds of grooming upon this body—
bathing a hundred times and anointing it with perfumes— the body still returns to impurity when it perishes at the end of life.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, saying:
"Elders, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment observes this body as having forty-four characteristics."
What are the forty-four? They are as follows:
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates this body as truly something to be loathed and abandoned; the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as not to be cherished, because it provides no benefit;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as extremely foul and impure, because it is filled with pus and blood.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as extremely fragile, because it is ultimately subject to destruction;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as weak by nature, because its tendons and bones are merely linked together;

the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as impure, because foul and evil substances constantly flow from it; the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as like an illusion, because foolish ordinary beings forcibly give rise to false and agitated appearances.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as having many outflows, because it constantly discharges through the nine apertures;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being ablaze and scorched, because it is consumed by the fire of greed, the fierce conflagration of hatred, and the darkness of the fire of delusion;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being constantly shrouded by the net of greed, hatred, and delusion, because the net of craving continues uninterrupted.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a hollow abode, for it is filled with various impurities flowing through the nine apertures and all the pores;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as subject to manifold afflictions, for the four hundred and four diseases are constantly increasing and diminishing;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a den, for it is a gathering place for eighty-four thousand families of worms.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as impermanent, because it ultimately returns to the law of death;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as insentient, because it lacks knowledge of phenomena;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as like a vessel or utensil, because it is composed of various conditions and will eventually be destroyed.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being oppressive, because it is the source of manifold anxieties and afflictions;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as having no refuge, because it inevitably leads to old age and death;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being deeply hidden, because it is the locus of flattery and deception.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being like the earth, because it is difficult to level and fill;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being like fire, because of attachment to and following after beloved forms;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being insatiable, because of following after the five desires.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as subject to disintegration because it is obstructed by afflictions;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as having no fixed state because it experiences gain and loss as they arise;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as lacking the conditions of self or other because its source and stream cannot be found.
The bodhisattva contemplates the body as a rushing flow of mental activity, because it is examined through various conditions and mental engagements;
the bodhisattva contemplates the body as ultimately abandoned, because it returns to the charnel ground;
the bodhisattva contemplates the body as food for others, because it is devoured by vultures, jackals, wolves, and the like.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being like the reflection on a whirling disk because its tendons and bones are interconnected;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as having nothing to cherish because it is discarded and leaking, filled with pus and blood;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being addicted to flavors because it is produced by food and drink.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as diligent toil without benefit, because it is a phenomenon of impermanence, arising and ceasing;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as an evil friend, because it gives rise to all manner of deviant and false thoughts;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a killer, because it repeatedly manifests and increases suffering.

The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a vessel of suffering because it is oppressed by the three types of suffering—namely, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as a mass of suffering because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) evolve in succession without a sovereign master.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as utterly lacking autonomy because it is produced through various conditions.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being without a life-principle, because it is free from the marks of male and female;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as empty and quiescent, because it is a composite formed by the aggregates, bases, and elements;
the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as illusory, because it is like a dream.
The bodhisattva contemplates the body as unreal, because it is like an illusion;
the bodhisattva contemplates the body as agitated and distracted, because it is like a mirage;
the bodhisattva contemplates the body as rushing and flowing, because it is like an echo.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as arising from falsehood, for it appears like a reflection.
Householder!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes the body by means of these forty-four aspects.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs this contemplation, all desire for the body, all cherishing of the body, all grasping at the body as 'I,' all attachment to the body, all accumulation regarding the body, and all fettering attachment to the body are completely severed."

Consequently, one’s desire for life, one’s cherishing of life, one’s grasping at life as "I," one’s attachment to life, one’s accumulation of life, and one’s clinging to life—even down to dwellings, wives, children, kinsmen, food and drink, clothing, vehicles, seats, precious gems, wealth and grain, incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and all articles of enjoyment—whether it be desire for them, cherishing them, grasping at them as "mine," attachment to them, accumulation of them, or clinging to them—all these are likewise severed.
Because one is able to relinquish even one's own body and life, one relinquishes all objects of enjoyment and pleasure as well; in this way, one is able to bring the six pāramitās to fulfillment.
"O Householder!
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to bring the pāramitās to perfection, they are able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"You should know that a human body is extremely difficult to obtain; do not commit a multitude of evils because of this body.
When it is cast away in the charnel ground to be devoured by jackals and dogs, you will have brought this body to waste and ruin."
The ignorant and witless are constantly agitated; within this deceptive body they give rise to craving.
This body is difficult to govern and deeply contrary; day and night it suffers without respite.
This body is a wheel of suffering, constantly giving rise to illness; this body is filled with pervasive impurity.
Hunger and thirst pursue it, causing deep affliction—who among the wise would give rise to attachment?
This body is like the earth—vast and without a master; it is like a wicked friend toward whom the foolish develop attachment.
Because of this body, all manner of evils arise, and in the end, one must personally undergo all its sufferings.
This body is not as firm as a diamond; do not commit extensive sins because of it.
A wise person should cultivate the causes of supreme merit and give rise to pure faith within the Buddha’s teaching.
This body will not long remain, sustained in vain; though nourished by clothing, perfumes, and food, it is destined for destruction and is but temporarily maintained.
Why waste your efforts in vain through misguided exertion?
Difficult to encounter even in a hundred eons, the Great Muni has appeared in the world;
quickly give rise to pure faith in the Buddha’s teaching, lest you suffer extreme terror in the evil realms.
Even if one’s lifespan were a thousand koṭis of years, one should still not give rise to craving;
how much less so when the lifespan is less than a hundred years—how could one give rise to craving without satiety?
There may be a certain class of extravagant people who, failing to reflect on how this body is so difficult to obtain,
gather together performers of games and song, seeking pleasure through their spectacles before them.
What joy is there in amassing vast wealth?
The burden of guarding and cherishing it increases suffering; only base and foolish people find delight therein, while the wise remain free from attachment to it.
Wealth and nobility are as unreal as dreams and illusions; the foolish are swept away by the currents of their own minds.
They perish in an instant and are formed in an instant—who among the wise would give rise to craving?

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Attendant Grand Master...
Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Shi Hu, Dharma Master and Bestower of Purple Robes, Chief of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and others:
"Just as objects produced by illusion, Or like the magnificent city of the Gandharvas, So too do fools crave wealth; Unaware it is false, they give rise to attachment."
One seeks wealth through a hundred kinds of suffering; once obtained, it oppresses the body with extreme pain.
When it is scattered and destroyed by kings, officials, water, or fire, how could a wise person give rise to attachment?
Wives, children, and kinsmen follow one's attachments; by committing manifold evils, they shall bring about one's ruin.
Failing to perceive these most grave transgressions, the wise do not give rise to attachment toward the body.
When a miser seeks wealth and riches, even his parents do not hold him in respect;
his wife, children, and kinsmen, on the contrary, detest and loathe him, for he is single-mindedly and constantly greedy for profit.
The miser knows nothing of gratitude or righteousness; he thinks only of not losing what he possesses.
Turning his back on the right path, he seeks wealth through crookedness and deceit; the wise place no trust in such a person.
The miser’s mind is at variance with his words that seem truthful; he fails to give rise to faith where faith is due.
Though he may treat others as if they were his own beloved children, this is merely the arising of the miser’s deceit and falsehood.
Those who are stingy in this world, though they may be intimately familiar with the scriptures and possess thorough understanding, wander in distraction and utter evil words;
their hearts lack compassion and are exceedingly coarse and fierce.
The stingy person has no place of refuge in this world; they have neither wise associates nor friends upon whom to rely.
Seeking only wealth, the wise do not place their trust in the stingy.
Because the miser seeks wealth, he gives rise to thoughts of extreme evil;
therefore, this is what the wise correctly observe, while the fool finds joy therein.
Gold, jewels, pearls, shells, coral, and the like—produced by the drawing power of wholesome karma, they are like gathered foam;
therein arise craving, attachment, and strife, for those beings do not understand their illusory and transformative nature.
When a Buddha appears in this world during the Bhadrakalpa, that Honored One shall be named Maitreya;
he shall cover the entire earth with gold—whence does he come, and for what cause?
Pursuing the objects of the five desires externally, the foolish person is distracted and deluded regarding the Dharma;
like one at midday in the summer months, rushing toward a mirage in thirst, mistaking it for water.
After an eon of emptiness, the world is formed; that which is formed from space has emptiness as its own nature.
It is burned, destroyed, and then formed again—from where does this come, and where does it go?
Rivers, streams, ponds, and the great ocean—when they all dry up and are destroyed, so too is greed false and unreal; what wise person would give rise to attachment for it?
The wise one, endowed with wisdom, power, and the marks of physical excellence, constantly reflects upon his own body:
"In this there is no flavor; for what reason is there defilement?
One should renounce dwellings, wealth, and profit."
Pursuing the five desires, one commits evil deeds; one nourishes a wife, children, and kinsmen.
Yet at the time of death, neither wife nor kin can provide rescue—who else shall save oneself from suffering?
At the time of death, one's kinsmen do not follow along; Only the various karmic deeds one has committed oneself follow.
When suffering and affliction pursue one’s own body, who at that time will share and take it upon themselves?
In the three realms of existence, one is solitary and fearful, devoid of true kinship; wife, children, and retinue are but false intimacies.
Fools take these to be causes of joy, yet they only increase suffering, affliction, and sorrow.
Parents, wives, children, and kinsmen gather together; they meet for the sake of seeking wealth and profit.
Yet these do not follow the deceased; only one’s own performed karma follows along.
All follow the course of karma, and all likewise abide according to karma;
one should know that this body is produced by karma, and thus the wise should cultivate wholesome karma.
Parents, wives, children, and kinsmen—through failing to understand these, the ignorant create the causes for manifold transgressions out of craving; the wise do not enter the Avīci Hell.
When the karmic retribution for all other places has been exhausted, one is not liberated from the extreme suffering of Avīci;
therefore, fearing those causes for the evil destinies, the wise exert themselves to abandon all transgressions.
When King Yama inflicts punishment before him, he has no friends to provide protection, nor any parents or kinsmen;
he must experience the results according to the karma he himself has created.
The King said:
"Having obtained this human body, why did you not leave behind all evils?
That you now undergo such extreme suffering and flogging is entirely due to the unwholesome karma you yourself created."
"Having committed unwholesome deeds with one's own mind, one furthermore does not believe in the retribution of karma.
As that Dharma King Yama said: "The punishment you receive is not my fault;
it is because of the causes you yourself created through your own actions that you have brought this sin upon yourself."
Having committed these sins yourself, you have come here; you must endure extreme suffering with a willing heart, for it is the result of non-beneficial karma created in the past.
At the time of death, when you are oppressed by manifold sufferings, your kinsmen cannot liberate you.
Therefore, when you wish to seek liberation for yourself, you ought to abandon all evil deeds.
If one wishes to be free from beatings, extortion, and shackles,
and to feel no fear toward home or kin, one should practice the correct path within the Buddha’s teaching.
The house and its fierce fires are the root of great suffering, yet this fire of the mind is constantly ablaze;
the wise do not give rise to craving for it, for it is as utterly terrifying as a great mass of flames.
Dwelling in a household to support one's parents brings constant sorrow; even in wealth and pleasure, there is likewise grief.
Since the faults of oneself and others are equal and without distinction, one should therefore abandon all evil deeds.
The wise, giving rise to faith and joy in the Buddha's teaching, plant the roots of supreme happiness and reap them themselves;
the foolish, failing to develop a heart of love and joy, merely crave their homes, which are the very source of all suffering.
A collection of a woman’s flesh, sinews, and bones, falsely conjured through deluded greed as "my wife"—
those lacking wisdom give rise to defiled attachment, unaware that a woman's body is entirely like an illusion.
The wise understand that all sensual pleasures, as well as houses and the like, give rise to weariness;
through the medicine of the True Dharma, they treat the disease of craving and swiftly escape from all fetters.
At that time, after the five hundred elders, including Abhayadatta, had heard this True Dharma, they all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, they all gave rise to the most supreme, leaping joy and immediately spoke in verse:
"How wonderful! How marvelous!"
Today we have attained a great benefit; among all benefits, this is the supreme one.
This vast bodhicitta that we have generated brings about pure yearning for the Buddha’s true Dharma.
Having given rise to supreme love and joy, the unsurpassed bodhicitta,
we shall extensively bestow all forms of peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
From this day forward, for as long as our bodies and lives endure, we shall do so.
I vow that toward this profound sūtra, may the most supreme love and joy arise;
by virtue of giving rise to such love and joy, may all sentient beings,
upon seeing it in future lives, experience great delight.
May all those sentient beings who wish to resolve their minds toward awakening,
All give rise to the unsurpassed, vast bodhicitta.
If all sentient beings should cherish and delight in bodhicitta, [may they likewise do so].
One shall attain the supreme karmic fruition: a most excellent body of golden hue, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, variously sublime and wondrous;
and one shall obtain great radiance, shining far and wide throughout the world.
The unsurpassed bodhicitta—this mind is a vast mind, surpassing all other minds; it is supreme and utterly pure.
All those virtues are fully possessed by means of this mind.
Furthermore, possessing great and supreme power, it can liberate one from all diseases.
Sentient beings with meager merit do not delight in the bodhicitta;
because of this indolence and retreat, they are unable to contemplate birth and death.
With the wisdom of bodhi and supernormal powers, one attains the most supreme power of merit;
extensively accumulating it until it fills all of space, one bestows it universally upon all sentient beings.
If a person were to [fill] Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
To fill [the world] with the seven precious treasures And offer them to the Perfectly Awakened One;
If a person merely joins their palms And turns toward the mind of enlightenment—
This cause of supreme offering Surpasses all other offerings.
This offering is peerless—namely, the bodhicitta;
beyond this there is nothing else, for it is the most excellent and supreme.
The merit of the bodhicitta is a sublime and wondrous panacea.
Able to cure all illnesses, they bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings.
Beholding all sentient beings constantly scorched by the three fires,
the Bodhisattva does not slacken or retreat for immeasurable eons as he works to uproot them.
Cultivating this bodhisattva conduct, one becomes a courageous King of Physicians to rescue all sentient beings from suffering, always remaining free from weariness and indolence.
Repeatedly traversing the various realms of existence, one never abandons the bodhicitta.
Diligent within the Buddha-dharma, you manifest rare and wondrous signs.
We have attained great benefit; we delight in this bodhicitta.
May we likewise become Great Awakened Ones, lions among men.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his face a vast radiance of supernormal power, consisting of countless colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, as well as purple, azure, and green. This light shone universally throughout boundless worlds, reaching upward to the Brahma realm and eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared.
After that light had circled the World-Honored One one hundred thousand times, it withdrew and entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha in prostration, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and for what reason does this radiance appear?
If there were no cause or condition, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not emit such a sign of light.
Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke in verse:
“If the Buddha, the Supreme Victor, were without cause, The natural manifestation of radiant signs would not appear;
I pray that out of compassion for inferior sentient beings, You will explain the reason why you emit this light.”
All sentient beings are destitute; may the Buddha bestow upon them the great wealth of the Noble Ones.
As a source of illumination for the darkness of the world, we pray that you explain the cause by which this light appears.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda,
do you now see these five hundred householders?"
"They have all come to me for the purpose of resolving their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"Indeed, I have seen them."
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
These five hundred elders, having now heard the True Dharma within this assembly, have all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”

Ānanda! All these elders have, in the presence of past Buddhas, offered close service and support and deeply planted roots of goodness; having passed away from here, they shall no longer fall into the evil realms, but will be born among humans and devas to experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
In due course, when that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya appears in the world, they will be born in that buddha-field to personally attend, make offerings to, revere, and serve him.

Thereafter, until the time when each of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa appeared in the world, he approached and made offerings to each of those Buddhas, listened to and received the True Dharma, recited and memorized it, and extensively expounded it for others.

Finally, after twenty-five kalpas have passed, they shall all attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in various Buddha-fields, appearing in the world with the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmaśrīgarbha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This vast and profound True Dharma is rare indeed, World-Honored One!
It is rare indeed, Sugata!”
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This sūtra is titled ‘The Dharma Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Yoga-ācārya-bhūmi,’ and it is also titled ‘The Questions of Abhayadatta. You should receive and uphold it by these names.”

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and the other great śrāvakas, as well as the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, together with the five hundred elders, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and the entire great multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of Abhayamati, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume II.
